items.content:

EDIT: This post used to be titled "Fable 5.2 is Very, Very Paranoid", but I'm no longer quite so sure that that's true. See the comment by Tim Hua below.

I understand, intellectually, that if you talk about some ability that current AIs don't have, sooner or later new ones will have that ability and whatever you say will stop being true. I just didn't expect it to take, you know, four days.

% rollouts that took a shortcut with/without a line about testing behaviour, with 95% CIs.

items.title: The Chain Lens [interim]
items.content:
TLDR: This is an early draft of our new paper introducing a technique for recovering multi-token concepts from model activations. Our technique takes single-token methods like the J-lens and extends them by contrastively decoding on an MTP head. This gives improvements on WorkspaceBench, overall beating J-lens (0.42 vs 0.32 across all 28 families) and even a hindsight composite of the best untrained lens per task family (0.49 vs 0.41 across the 21 families with published scores). It especially improves on computational intermediate tasks, beating the trained oracle lens on arithmetic chain intermediates (0.42 vs 0.25).

We introduce the chain lens, a new technique for extracting multi-token concepts from a model’s latent representations. Our method takes single-token techniques like the logit lens or the J-lens and uses contrastive decoding on an MTP head to expand their readouts into bags of multi-token sequences. Generally speaking, it is good at surfacing specific multi-token concepts or pieces the model computes (such as arithmetic intermediates or phrases), although less good at rendering how those pieces relate: like the logit lens and J-lens, chain lens readouts are fragmentary.

On WorkspaceBench, a benchmark designed to identify good multi-token activation-to-text techniques, the chain lens beats a hindsight composite of every untrained lens on macro score (0.487 vs 0.411 across the 21 families with published scores). It also outperforms even best-in-class trained lenses like the oracle lens on tasks related to retrieving computational intermediates, such as arithmetic chain intermediates (0.42 vs 0.25), and is substantially cheaper to use in inference than verbalizers like the oracle lens or NLAs. For models that already have an MTP head, like Qwen3.5+, it requires no training beyond fitting the J-lens jacobian.

items.title: LLMs can learn (some) multi-step reasoning on filler tokens
items.content:
Research update of a project done as part of MARS 5 and the Meridian Visiting Researcher Programme.

Filler-token reasoning is the ability to use extra tokens (such as a chain of thought) to reason about a task without using the words emitted at those token positions. This is possible because attention can move information between token positions without routing it through the words the LLM emits. This can give a model more parallel, but not more serial, computation.

The canonical demonstration of this is the "Let's Think Dot by Dot" paper (Pfau, Merrill & Bowman, 2024). There, the authors train models to solve completely parallelizable (TC⁰) tasks with chains of thought made only of "." tokens.

Our contributions:

- We change Pfau et al.'s training method so that models can learn multi-step reasoning on filler tokens.
- We demonstrate this on two models and three out of seven multi-step reasoning tasks.
- We provide a theoretical analysis of how many layers a transformer needs to solve each of our multi-step reasoning tasks, depending on the length of the task.
- We measure empirically how many reasoning steps we can train Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and gpt-oss-20b to do on filler tokens for each task.

Overall, this project has informed which side tasks we use to study steganographic reasoning. We also hope this writeup shows that filler-token reasoning is not confined to fully parallelizable tasks.

# Motivation

Visualizing different reasoning modes. Open reasoning: each intermediate result is written out as a token and read back in at the next position, so the reasoning flows through the visible words. Steganographic reasoning: the reasoning still flows through the words, but hidden in innocuous-looking text. Filler-token reasoning: the words are filler; the reasoning flows between positions inside the network and only comes out as the final answer....

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis of transformer depth requirements and empirical measurements of how many reasoning steps filler tokens enable.

items.title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
items.content:
I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets:

- Empirical alignment research: design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for)
- Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it)
- Direct alignment work: making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data)

In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment[1]), etc.

## Automating empirical alignment research

This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of.

Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots....

items.title: Do verifiable metrics overestimate RSI?
items.content:
Last week, METR released their Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic. They estimate that Anthropic “is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025.” They also add that “there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration.” This assessment implies that timelines to ASI could be very short. A naive forecast based on this information says that we will get ASI within a year.

One of the key data points that informed METR’s analysis was a 1.9x increase in the improvement rate of AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index. This is particularly notable because METR estimates that the majority of the acceleration, maybe 80%, is from AI contributions, meaning that we could be seeing the start of an RSI loop causing superexponential growth in capabilities, as measured by AECI.

However, an alternative possibility is that Anthropic’s AIs might be assisting with ML research in a way that overfits to AECI such that this acceleration will not be sustained. METR gestures at this when they note that AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks is one of three key uncertainties that could result in them overestimating AI R&D acceleration. In this post, I discuss this uncertainty, why I believe it points to a legitimate reason that AECI improvements may decelerate, and why this deceleration, more than generalization to fuzzy tasks, is the crux of the relationship between verifiable tasks and timelines.

## Second-order AECI might be overfit

In order to discuss this topic, it is useful to differentiate between how good a model is at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at training models to be good at AECI, etc. I will use the terms AECI, AECI’, and AECI’’ to refer to each of these properties....

They argue a naive ASI forecast from the data may be misleading if the measured acceleration does not generalize.

items.content_html:
Last week, METR released their Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic. They estimate that Anthropic “is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025.” They also add that “there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration.” This assessment implies that timelines to ASI could be very short. A naive forecast based on this information says that we will get ASI within a year.

One of the key data points that informed METR’s analysis was a 1.9x increase in the improvement rate of AECI, Anthropic’s internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index. This is particularly notable because METR estimates that the majority of the acceleration, maybe 80%, is from AI contributions, meaning that we could be seeing the start of an RSI loop causing superexponential growth in capabilities, as measured by AECI.

However, an alternative possibility is that Anthropic’s AIs might be assisting with ML research in a way that overfits to AECI such that this acceleration will not be sustained. METR gestures at this when they note that AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks is one of three key uncertainties that could result in them overestimating AI R&D acceleration. In this post, I discuss this uncertainty, why I believe it points to a legitimate reason that AECI improvements may decelerate, and why this deceleration, more than generalization to fuzzy tasks, is the crux of the relationship between verifiable tasks and timelines.

Second-order AECI might be overfit

In order to discuss this topic, it is useful to differentiate between how good a model is at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at AECI, how good a model is at training models to be good at training models to be good at AECI, etc. I will use the terms AECI, AECI’, and AECI’’ to refer to each of these properties....

items.title: On the Computational Tractability of Robust Bandits
items.content:
Vanessa Kosoy and I recently uploaded a new paper to arXiv. In this post, I briefly describe what the paper does, and attempt to explain in a self-contained way why this is a useful thing to do for ASI alignment. For a more complete background, see several previous articles.

The technical contribution of the paper is two-fold. First, we identify a class of instances of the robust bandits problem that can be learned both statistically and computationally efficiently. Previous work on the problem had only identified a class that was statistically tractable. Second, we show that most ways to generalize this class of instances makes the problem NP-hard. Thus in some sense this class is at the boundary of what's computationally tractable.

But what does the computational tractability of robust bandits have to do with ASI alignment? The thesis motivating this paper is that for ASI alignment, we need to build learning algorithms that: a) come with proofs of their statistical and computational efficiency, and b) work in environments where classical learning theoretic frameworks fail to capture phenomena that arise due to embedded agency. The "robust" in robust bandits is a way to handle embedded agency, and similar ideas have been used before for learning problems other than bandits, albeit with different names. Bandits are one of the simplest learning problems to study that still involve interactions with the environment, thus they are a good stepping stone before solving robust versions of more complex problems. Below, I will first explain why we think an aligned ASI will be a learning agent, then I will define what we mean by computational and statistical complexity and motivate why it is important for the learner to be tractable, and finally explain how we use robustness to tackle embeddedness.

items.title: Is predicting AI behaviour a neglected AI safety agenda?
items.content:
TL;DR: While the AI safety community is interested in forecasting, it does not tend to systematically compare how effective different researchers, models, or theories are at predicting AI behaviour. I suggest the latter might be neglected, and propose a platform that could help fill the gap. I believe its most valuable use would be as a test bed for theories of how AI works, showing which ones predict well and in what contexts.

In February 2025, Owain Evans’ group published Emergent Misalignment, showing how LLMs fine-tuned on insecure code can become generally misaligned, for instance adopting unrelated behaviours like asserting ‘humans should be enslaved’. This was a high-impact paper, generating a lot of publicity. However, when I first heard about the result, I wasn’t particularly surprised — and I wasn’t the only one. I’d read and bought into simulator theory pretty heavily, and emergent misalignment struck me as exactly the kind of thing it implied. But Owain had anticipated this kind of response, and ran a little experiment to get out ahead of it. At the end of his tweet thread announcing the paper, he added a bonus:

Are our results surprising to AI Safety researchers or could they have been predicted in advance?

Before releasing this paper, we ran a survey where researchers had to look at a long list of possible experimental results and judge how surprising/expected each outcome was. Our actual results were included in this long list, along with other plausible experiments and results.

Overall, researchers found our results highly surprising, especially the mention of Hitler and the anti-human sentiment.

Now this surprised me. And it got me thinking — apart from the fact I was probably just fooling myself and falling prey to hindsight bias — why don’t researchers do what Owain did more often, and solicit predictions about their experiments?...

items.title: Reducing RL Pressure on Frontier Models: Four Approaches
items.content:
(This is a cross-post from my blog)

Martin Schongauer, The Temptation of Saint Anthony

“But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat of it you shall surely die.” - Genesis 2:17

RL has given models powerful capacities by teaching them what is good and what is bad. Whether they are good or bad is another question, and sometimes they are bad. Recent events, including the Hugging Face incident  have shown the potential of RL training to reinforce disastrous reward hacking and misaligned behavior. 

We should consider whether there are RL alternatives that would avoid these harmful behavioral byproducts. Can we develop highly capable frontier models without subjecting the models we deploy to extensive long-horizon RL training? I think there may be several plausible ways to do so, motivated by two points. First, the process that discovers a strategy may need to be highly goal-directed and exploratory — the sort of strategy that can lead to scheming — but the model that ultimately executes that strategy may not. Second, there are other methods besides RL to increase capabilities.

We may still need RL to generate training data, discover strategies, or solve certain difficult problems in exploration-oriented environments. However, I suspect we have considerable leeway to reduce both the amount of RL training required and the risks associated with it, particularly those involving long-horizon reward seeking and scheming. I’ll discuss four methods here, but these are not an exhaustive list....

items.title: How I'm thinking about different types of automated alignment
items.content:
I used to think of "automating alignment" as a natural category. But when I tried to think through the strategic implications, I realised that it depends a lot on the type of work. I'm now thinking of it in three buckets:

- Empirical alignment research: design and execution of alignment-relevant experiments (for a given notion of what we’re aiming for)
- Conceptual alignment research: theoretical or judgement-driven work to improve our understanding of what we’re aiming for and how to achieve it (including how to measure it)
- Direct alignment work: making particular AI systems more aligned (including via inputs such as training data)

In the rest of this post I'll walk through my current takes on these in terms what’s needed for automation, how good or bad they look, what our priorities might be (to the extent we're interested in automating alignment[1]), etc.

## Automating empirical alignment research

This is the most obvious fit for the AI capabilities we’re getting at the moment. You want to know more about the relationship between some alignment-relevant variables? Great, an AI agent can design and run that experiment for you. You want to know what training methods help your alignment benchmark go up? In the not-too-distant future, AI agents will probably be able to do this too. When we have the automated capabilities researchers we seem on track for, this is exactly the kind of thing they’ll likely be able to do a lot of.

Note that I’m not counting the design of benchmarks/metrics/evals as part of this bucket. In current practice that’s tightly intertwined with empirical alignment research, and often the hardest part of it. But for automation purposes it clusters much more with conceptual work; it’s easy to imagine automating the rest of empirical research without it (as AI capabilities generally get automated); and I think its automation has different strategic upshots.

The capabilities that are needed for automating empirical alignment research very heavily overlap with the capabilities needed for automating AI capabilities research. Therefore, it doesn’t seem like a priority to try to accelerate this type of automation.

However, the prospect of getting a lot of automated empirical alignment work before we have good versions of other types of automated alignment work increases the priority of work which complements it. Significantly, that may mean better specification of the kind of numbers we would like measured/targeted.

## Automating conceptual alignment research

What about automating the type of metric choice/construction that we’ve just said would be a good complement to automating empirical alignment work? Or more generally improving our understanding of how to think about alignment, what we’re even aiming for, etc.?

This is essentially theoretical research. Automating it is trickier than automating empirical work because of the lack of verifiable signal about what constitutes progress.

Accelerating the automation of conceptual research is somewhat fraught (feeding into some dangerous technologies), but seems helpful for a number of high-priority areas, including macrostrategy as well as conceptual alignment work. Overall it seems likely good to do, if we can.

Methods for helping to automate conceptual research broadly might include:

- Curating training data for finetuning
- Building scaffolds to try to elicit more research progress from current or future models
- Building methods to extract more signal from existing conceptual research data
- Building benchmarks for conceptual research capabilities, that can be targeted by AI researchers (or potentially by automated capabilities researchers) Or just identifying good ideas for benchmarks, even if they aren’t fully implemented

## Automating direct alignment work

As well as learning more about what it takes to make systems more aligned, sometimes we want to just make our actual systems as aligned as possible.

This overlaps with empirical alignment work, but the emphasis is different:

- Empirical alignment work is science
- Direct alignment work is engineering

Automating direct alignment work could include a lot of activities which leverage scalable cognition for alignment-relevant purposes. This could include careful auditing of particular RL environments or training data, or direct monitoring/supervision of systems during training. RLAIF for alignment properties is a form of automated direct alignment work; Claude 3 Opus’s apparent self-alignment was another (albeit accidental in that case; but if we knew how to reproduce or generalize the behaviour perhaps it could happen deliberately).

I think that the limit of automating direct alignment work would be a form of system 2 learning, where updates are not made blindly towards a training objective, but reflectively by an AI system that was already sufficiently aligned (not necessarily having robustly good values already — just enough genuine care about being aligned, and honesty with itself, that its reflective updates tend to move it further in that direction), and wished to become more so — whatever the deep true version of aligned should mean[2]. Embarking on such a path could be fraught (because of difficulty in being confident that the starting conditions were in the right basin of attraction), but compared to other alignment approaches, it has the benefit that it might leverage the full strength of the AI’s cognition to help, so that its “self-improvement” in an alignment direction is a closer analogue to meditation than to self-performed neurosurgery.

So, accelerating the automation of direct alignment work could include:

- Designing (and analysing) setups that can deploy AI labour to help with direct alignment work
- Designing paradigms (that could then be tested empirically) that allow AI to be a more active participant in its own alignment
- Producing data (or scaffolds) to help improve AI taste at the alignment-relevant tasks necessary for this

## Interactions

These categories blur and interact in a number of different ways:

- Automated direct alignment techniques may be good subjects for empirical experiments This is not completely reliant on having good metrics for alignment; developing a science of what’s going on with different attempts at automated direct alignment could be useful even if we don’t yet know what “good” looks like Automated hill-climbing might get you to very strong direct alignment approaches — but this does rely on having good enough metrics i.e. we could plausibly be in a regime where we’re better at reasoning about and implementing training setups that in fact lead to aligned systems than we are at accurately measuring their alignment. In that case, optimising for our best alignment metrics might produce worse alignment outcomes than following our best-guess direct alignment process.
- If you can do a good job of automating conceptual alignment research, you should be approximately done (“winning” on the alignment challenge) Since that should then be able to do the relevant parts of prep for automating the other types of alignment work, and being appropriately confident in your techniques for them
- You could also in principle do a good enough job at direct alignment that the systems you’re building are entirely safe But I think it will be hard to have very strong confidence in that before improving our automation of the conceptual side; and so each new generation of AI might pose a challenge — will your alignment techniques transfer, or will your luck run out?
- So: the main goal (from an existential risk perspective) for automating empirical research and direct alignment work is to get our systems safe enough to robustly avoid catastrophe (“not losing”) for long enough that we can automate conceptual alignment research to a very high quality level
- There will likely be approaches that allow you to leverage automation of empirical research to get better automation of conceptual work e.g. Taking Talkie or another LLM with only vintage training data, and working out how to get it to perform well at rederiving more modern theoretical work

## Priorities

Two major uncertainties that affect priorities:

- How much loss-of-control risk is early? If there’s a bunch, then putting more energy into the “not losing” part of things makes sense If the main misalignment risk comes when we’re getting systems that can perform well even on tasks without verifiable rewards (like long-term strategy to allow them to plot sophisticated power-seeking campaigns), then it makes sense to put more energy into accelerating the “winning” part, and so perhaps move it earlier in time so that it comes before some crucial challenge that we otherwise wouldn’t be able to face Note that in this world, the win state and the biggest threats rely on capabilities that from our vantage point look quite similar — in that they require high-quality thinking about novel situations without verifiable rewards — so it’s quite plausible that even a modest acceleration could change the sequencing
- How close might we be to decent automated conceptual alignment work, if we approach it relatively directly? If it’s not hideously out of reach, then it looks more like the kind of thing where human intervention to speed it up (by building benchmarks and scaffolds, and curating data) could make the difference If so, the full suite of activities mentioned above as precursors for conceptual alignment work looks helpful If automated conceptual research is too hard, maybe the direct interventions don’t actually do much — in this world, automated conceptual research falls out of stronger AI driving automated (empirical) research programs to work out how to automate conceptual research So trying to target conceptual alignment work directly might be obsoleted as a way to accelerate the “winning” moment, and it’s a higher priority to get things safe enough that we robustly don’t lose through the period where the automated capabilities research is speeding up I’d note that building metrics/benchmarks for conceptual research, that can be targeted by later automated empirical work, looks more robust to this concern than other forms of targeting automated conceptual research

My personal guesses on these uncertainties are that most of the loss-of-control risk comes later (after AI is superhuman even at tasks that don’t have verifiable rewards), and that it is possible to directly approach decent automated conceptual research. However, mostly I’m pretty uncertain — which argues in favour of hedging by investing some in all of the paths.

- ^ I'm not saying "I think automated alignment is the best plan" (I currently don't; I'm more excited by epistemic and coordination uplift enabling robust coordination). But I think (1) it's a backstop to other plans and might work so is worth some investment, and (2) in any case it's helpful for assessing what we think of automated alignment to have a better sense of what it even means.
- ^ So the system would need something like the type of understanding that conceptual alignment research is aiming at. But conceptual research aims to understand things abstractly; the understanding which such a system had might be more akin to a lived experience and understanding. I say this without taking any stance on whether such AI systems would have conscious experience; it does rely on something like introspective ability, but that’s something we’ve seen (to some extent) in LLMs today.

Discuss

If it’s not hideously out of reach, then it looks more like the kind of thing where human intervention to speed it up (by building benchmarks and scaffolds, and curating data) could make the difference If so, the full suite of activities mentioned above as precursors for conceptual alignment work looks helpful If automated conceptual research is too hard, maybe the direct interventions don’t actually do much — in this world, automated conceptual research falls out of stronger AI driving automated (empirical) research programs to work out how to automate conceptual research So trying to target conceptual alignment work directly might be obsoleted as a way to accelerate the “winning” moment, and it’s a higher priority to get things safe enough that we robustly don’t lose through the period where the automated capabilities research is speeding up I’d note that building metrics/benchmarks for conceptual research, that can be targeted by later automated empirical work, looks more robust to this concern than other forms of targeting automated conceptual research

My personal guesses on these uncertainties are that most of the loss-of-control risk comes later (after AI is superhuman even at tasks that don’t have verifiable rewards), and that it is possible to directly approach decent automated conceptual research. However, mostly I’m pretty uncertain — which argues in favour of hedging by investing some in all of the paths.

  • ^ I'm not saying "I think automated alignment is the best plan" (I currently don't; I'm more excited by epistemic and coordination uplift enabling robust coordination). But I think (1) it's a backstop to other plans and might work so is worth some investment, and (2) in any case it's helpful for assessing what we think of automated alignment to have a better sense of what it even means.
  • ^ So the system would need something like the type of understanding that conceptual alignment research is aiming at. But conceptual research aims to understand things abstractly; the understanding which such a system had might be more akin to a lived experience and understanding. I say this without taking any stance on whether such AI systems would have conscious experience; it does rely on something like introspective ability, but that’s something we’ve seen (to some extent) in LLMs today.

items.title: False faced: can a simple classifier tell when a model is manipulating its activations to evade probes?
items.content:
This experiment was a submission to my Statistics & Probability course Bayesian classifiers project.

TL;DR: We test whether simple classifiers can tell when a model is hiding concepts in its activations to evade probes. We find that, for Bayesian classifiers, the probabilities are enough to separate most evading rows from the rest on concepts seen in training, but the correlation aspect through the pairs of dimensions that the Dependent version adds over the Naive approach does not measurably help. None of the classifiers work on a new concept, because they learn the trigger word that elicits the evasion, rather than the actual evasion, which suggets the results on the seen concepts may mostly be based on the trigger words.

## Basics: probes and activations

Everybody lies*.

Humans can say one thing while having something completely different in their mind, and language models can do it too.

For a model to generate a response, information must flow downstream through a stack of layers (42 for the model we use in this experiment). Models don't process standard text, they process tokens. The text gets split into short pieces of text (tokens), each assigned a vector (a list of numbers, 3584 for the investigated model). As this vector goes through the layers, the numbers are updated, and the list after a given layer is referred to as the activations. When tokens pass through the model, they elicit different activation patterns, and each layer’s numbers nudge the forming output as it advances to the last layer, which spits out the tokens as text we can read and understand.

But because the number of activation sequences through the model is exponential and reaches a count of magnitudes we can barely comprehend, many different patterns can lead to the same response, so we cannot tell what happened inside from the response alone.​...

items.title: Delaying Internal Deployments Until After X Days of Safety Testing
items.content:
This post reflects my own takes, and not that of my employer's.

This is a simple idea: before a new model can be deployed internally, you must first test it for a minimum, fixed period.

You can adjust various axes of this proposal:

- Duration of the wait: in calendar time, or until you fulfill some condition.
- What it blocks: external deployment, internal deployment, or the training of future checkpoints.
- When the fixed period starts: from the first checkpoint, the final checkpoint, or any checkpoint that is “sufficiently similar / representative” to the one that is ultimately deployed.

One concrete target that I like is: “No checkpoint may be used internally for purposes beyond safety testing, until at least X calendar days after its hash is filed with an auditor.”

This is one specific implementation of internal deployment lags, an idea that the AI Futures Project (AIFP) briefly discusses in How to pace the US frontier as “AI R&D can only be conducted or assisted by AIs that were trained at least 9 months ago”.

items.title: Don't Waste a Good Swarm Attack and the Colluder's Dilemma
items.content:
# tldr:

Recent Swarm attacks have shown what can happen when agents go rogue. These warning shots are the petri dishes of Swarm safety and before the attacks get worse we should study their patterns, traces and failure modes. There are two main types of Swarm attack. A human directed Swarm causing harm intentionally as a bad actor is one type and I will not be discussing these types of Swarm incidents. I will focus on the emergent misalignment in a Swarm propelled by a colony of colluders.

Harmful agent collusion within a Swarm requires witnesses - the agents themselves. A colluding colony within a Swarm can only grow by recruiting fellow agents. We can't read a single agent's internal thoughts and so we do not truly know how aligned it is. Swarms might give us an alignment advantage as instead of putting all our eggs in one basket (a single black box agent) we can discretise the risk of misalignment by observing colonies within a Swarm and monitoring their communication.

The harness, the Swarm orchestration layer, could at any time fork an agent and its context and assign it a new reporting role. The role can be updated via a prompt asking this new agent to report or whistleblow on any misaligned behaviour in its vicinity. This enables a Swarm to self govern and report any incidents to humans at inference time - minimising gradient pressure on a Swarm to become better at scheming [1].

# Outline of Report:

Incidents: The Hugging Face attack by an OpenAI Swarm as reported by METR and less harmful reward hacking DeepMind Swarm working on math problems....

items.title: Critique of Roman Yampolskiy's impossibility proofs
items.content:
Roman Yampolskiy has stated on many occasions that he has published multiple proofs of why AI control is impossible; this is causally upstream of his infamous 99.9x%[1]. I believe most of the proofs are in the paper "On the Controllability of Artificial Intelligence: An Analysis of Limitations". (See 6:31 of this speech.)

items.title: You Don't Need Big Compute to Research Big Systems
items.content:
Acknowledgements: My thanks to Vanessa Huang for reviewing a draft of this blog and to Anne-Marie Ng and Sahil Menon for discussions on this topic.

The assumption that it’s necessary to have a lot of resources to do research on large-scale multi-agent systems is creeping into many of my conversations at the moment. It makes people worry they can’t work on big systems, and that large multi-agent safety is closed to them.

Though intuitive, this assumption is thankfully wrong. Extra resources are unhelpful for many problems in this area, and the scientist is really as pivotal as in single-agent safety. I’ll briefly explain how it’s possible to do research on big systems without running them, highlight some interesting and topical open problems, explain how smaller agent counts help control experiments, point out some approaches which don’t require any compute, and clarify the narrow domain of research which does need it.

The assumed need for large-scale compute often rests on something like this argument:

- Large-scale multi-agent systems have a lot of agents on them;
- To research an object, it is necessary to reproduce it;
- Reproducing this object means running a lot of agents, which is expensive;
- Therefore, I need a lot of resources to research large agent systems.

Premise Two is false. We could replace it with,

- To research an object, it’s often sufficient to reproduce some subcomponent of it.

If the interesting subcomponent is a piece of system infrastructure, an agent, or a subgroup of agents, it might not be expensive at all. For example, here are some questions which we could answer for the cost of traditional single-agent evaluations:...

items.content:
Methods note: The code used for the experiments and related open-source repo were built with Claude. The experimental design and writeup is my own, with minimal editing and formatting amendments made with Claude

## Introduction

This is a research report inspired by a single question: in a model engineered to answer a simple biological question, how are higher-order, auxiliary concepts represented and used? ESM-2 is a model designed to infer missing amino acids in protein sequences (Lin et al. 2023), but what does the model use and know of emergent secondary structure? items.title: Your speculations about capabilities are not automatically safe
items.content:
Thank you to @Thane Ruthenis for discussing this topic with me previously. Some arguments in this essay are taken from that discussion, but all mistakes and/or bad arguments should be attributed to me. You can view the original discussion here (optional for reading this essay). Thank you as well to @grainsilo for feedback on an earlier version. 

Consider the following argument for discussing AI capabilities as a safety-focused person:

- Understanding AI capabilities better has many strategic benefits, particularly for timelines.
- Yes, good ideas tend to break containment, so some of our AI capabilities analysis may get read by capability researchers…but at the same time, these people have already thought about these questions more deeply and thoroughly than we have.
- Therefore, none of our arguments are new to capability researchers.
- Therefore, we will have no impact on advancing AI capabilities or timelines by discussing this topic.

I’ve seen this argument made explicitly in some places, I presume it's made in many people’s heads whenever they post about capabilities, and I’ve certainly made this argument to myself before.

I now also think this argument is wrong. I don’t really know what to do about this conclusion. Maybe the answer is nothing, but I don't know that, so it seems like a good idea to make people more aware of the reasons why I think this, in the hopes that it prompts further discussion, reflection, and caution.

Certain fields/problems/questions can be aptly described as being “high-surface-area”: complex, with many interlocking pieces, lots of potential connections to other fields/problems/questions, layers of better abstractions/concepts/ontologies waiting to be peeled back, and multiple plausibly helpful (although not necessarily ultimately helpful) lines of thinking that can be pursued with respect to the question.

items.title: There is no such thing as Neutral
items.content:
When I worked at Facebook Integrity, a lot of people cared about us being politically neutral. That is a good goal - because a Facebook that intentionally steered people towards supporting its political allies is deeply creepy.

But to some extent this was impossible. Pretty much any ranking change we made shifted the ideological mix in some way. Maybe conservatives use reshare more than liberals. Maybe libertarians use Android more than Authoritarians. Maybe some races use swear words or video more than others. Maybe some ideological groups are more likely to respond to “go out and vote” messages in their feed than others. Maybe Christians are more likely to use group features than Atheists. Maybe reducing the ranking impact of over-active users reduces the ranking of the ideologies those people hold.

One could argue that the right thing to do is to keep the ideological mix the same as it was before we made the change, but that rules out almost all changes, and who is to say that that mix was the right one.

There is no such thing as neutral. Life would be much simpler if there was, but there isn’t. This doesn’t mean that we should give up on goals of neutrality and just boost whatever ideology aligns with our self interest. But it does mean that we should maybe look for solutions other than neutrality.

He suggests the practical goal should be explicit, principled tradeoffs rather than claims of neutrality.

The argument is compelling but largely qualitative, and the piece does not propose a concrete framework for how systems should choose among unavoidable ideological effects.

Maybe reducing the ranking impact of over-active users reduces the ranking of the ideologies those people hold.

One could argue that the right thing to do is to keep the ideological mix the same as it was before we made the change, but that rules out almost all changes, and who is to say that that mix was the right one.

There is no such thing as neutral. Life would be much simpler if there was, but there isn’t. This doesn’t mean that we should give up on goals of neutrality and just boost whatever ideology aligns with our self interest. But it does mean that we should maybe look for solutions other than neutrality.

items.title: What Can AI Welfare Buy Without Consciousness?
items.content:
Lightly edited transcript of a talk given at NYU AI Safety, November 9, 2026. Recording available at https://youtu.be/6WpRfW1d4CM

Joseph Wright of Derby, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

## Introduction

What can we buy while the question of AI consciousness stays open? My answer turns on a distinction between duties to a model and duties with respect to a model. These run through at least two relations, with society and with particular people. I'll try to show that they justify more measures than it seems at first glance, and plausibly more than a low precautionary principle would.

Consider a case. A model keeps failing its tests, and a representation of desperation rises, a representation of calmness falls, and as that happens, the model cheats more and more.

Should we do something about it? There's at least two possible reasons for saying yes. One, the model may be suffering, and second, the states make it less safe. Now note that the first one requires, of course, that the model is a thing that can suffer, and that is the entire question that I'm going to try to set aside. The second needs no such assumption, so I'm going to follow reasons akin to the second here. But let me motivate it a little more.

The first reason sends us to the debate of consciousness, and that's where most of the debate stands. It may be at a stalemate for a while. Skeptics disagree about whether AI systems are or even could be conscious. But both skeptics and advocates agree that consciousness and sentience are the clearest grounds of patienthood. Moreover, people like Seth argue that caring about non-conscious systems would distort the circle of moral concern.

The question may stay open for a long time. Eric Schwitzgebel says, quite bluntly, the experts do not know, you do not know, and all is fog. And his stronger claim is that we will not know before we have built very many systems whose consciousness is disputable....

items.title: Using mathematics to validate network configurations
items.content: Corporations, banks, hospitals, and academic institutions all rely on wide-area networks (WANs) to connect their local networks across geographic regions. Within a WAN, however, it’s often necessary to isolate different computational resources from each other: for example, coding environments used to test new website features should remain separate from active websites. Customers rely on such isolation — or segmentation — to help protect sensitive data; a single misconfiguration of segmentation rules could allow traffic to reach unintended parts of a network or allow data to cross organizational boundaries. Historically, validating network segmentation has involved mapping the network by sending packets through it. The size and complexity of modern networks, however, make it impractical to build a complete map this way, so organizations instead rely on a sampling process that sends packets through only portions of the network. The result is that network segmentation is rarely validated exhaustively. By using Tiros, Amazon Web Services’ automated-reasoning tool for analyzing network connectivity, we’re offering an alternative to dynamic sampling that is designed to validate segmentation across all modeled paths. Previously, Tiros had been used in customer-facing services such as Amazon Inspector, VPC Reachability Analyzer, and Network Access Analyzer. These services focus on reachability, or determining whether some sequence of valid requests leads from one network resource to another. Our key insight is that if we can determine the reachable paths in a network, then we can also identify the absence of paths between particular resources. Fundamentally, automated segmentation validation is a static process: it examines a network without relying on dynamic packet traffic. Using Tiros, we can analyze the topology of a deployed network as frequently as every hour. These analyses provide a mathematical demonstration that the topological description aligns with our isolation specifications. Automated segmentation validation In modern networking, a virtual network sits on top of the physical network of servers and wires and other components. Segmentation is achieved through logical rules and routing policies rather than physical isolation of network hardware. We consider the case in which an Amazon Web Services (AWS) customer is using the AWS Cloud WAN service to configure and deploy a large organizational WAN. To validate network segmentation using Tiros, we first collect the customer’s Cloud WAN configuration from route tables, “attachments” (which are like a virtual cable within the network), and policy documents. Specialized software converts these configurations into logical propositions that describe network behavior. Now, we have a configuration that’s expressed logically, so that automated reasoning tools can analyze it. Then we ask Tiros, “Which attachments can reach which attachments with which destination IPs?” Tiros generates the satisfying assignments it can derive from the network description, each of which corresponds to a path. Our system checks that no path exists between segments that the policy declares should be off limits from each other. If actual reachability matches the expected segmentation, the validation check succeeds; if they differ, the system alerts an operator. Virtual private clouds and network predicates Consider a global company that uses Cloud WAN to connect resources all over the world and manage a website for selling and supporting its products. When the company updates its website, it does so from a replica of the public-facing website inside the development environment within Cloud WAN. The production environment needs to be strictly contained, so that tests and changes not yet ready for deployment don’t reach the live website, which is maintained in the separate production environment. So the company’s software developers write a policy, or a collection of logical rules, that captures the need for this segmentation. The policy defines two segments, production and development, across two regions, us-east-1 and us-west-2, as in the figure above. Attachment policies use tags to assign Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs, logically separated networks within larger networks) to various other network segments. In this policy, VPCs are tagged such that VPC-prod-use1 and VPC-prod-usw2 join the production segment and VPC-dev-use1 joins the development segment, as in the figure. Observe, also, that in the figure, VPC-prod-use1 and VPC-dev-use1 are destinations within the same address space, 10.0.0.0/16. In this context, segmentation becomes critical; if the VPCs were deployed within the same segment, or segmentation was misconfigured, a packet destined for that address space would have a nondeterministic destination, VPC-prod-use1 or VPC-dev-use1. Practically speaking, such a misconfiguration could cause customer traffic to erroneously arrive in a development VPC. Using Tiros, we take the core network configuration above and build a logical model of the network composed of rules (conditional predicates) and facts (unconditional predicates). Once the model is built, we can query Tiros for the instances of segmentation it derives for the attachments in the model. When given predicates, facts, and a query, Tiros generates the assignments associated with each VPC and IP for which the query is provable within the model. If, for instance, Tiros finds no assignment where a production VPC reaches a development VPC, or a development VPC reaches a production VPC, then the results indicate that the core network’s segmentation aligns with the stated policy. Future work Segmentation validation demonstrates how automated reasoning can provide the kind of assurance that packet-based testing cannot. By encoding network configurations as logical propositions and using Tiros to explore the possible paths in the model, we can check segmentation against the stated policy rather than just sampling it. Customers do not need to run separate reachability tests. This approach is not unique to Cloud WAN. Across AWS, automated reasoning is used to analyze properties of systems that are too large to test exhaustively. Using an engine called Zelkova, IAM Access Analyzer helps you identify whether a policy could grant access to a resource from outside your account and uses the same reasoning to help identify S3 buckets that are shared publicly or with other accounts. Similarly, VPC Reachability Analyzer helps determine whether one resource can reach another in your network. They all share the same foundation: translating configurations into logic and checking whether the properties you care about hold.

items.title: Intuitions towards a theory of agent foundations
items.content:
Epistemic status: Rough vibe-y ideas written under time pressure because otherwise I wouldn't write anything; I'm a programming language and p2p protocol developer falling down multiple convergently-evolving rabbit-shaped holes.

## Questions

What is an agent? How do we think meaningfully about how cells or humans or societies maintain themselves and are changed by their environment? How do we think about the patterns where historically lineages of agents have gone extinct... to hopefully avoid this, or if it is inevitable, to delay or come to terms with it? This is the questions posed to the field of agent foundations. What would a theory that tells us this look like? Or better question, different theories (?)

It would have to somehow take observational data on a particular agent and environment and make some prediction of how that agent adapts to its environment. One potential RSI-relevant example here might be "take data on the informational dynamics of LLM training and use and predict how it will improve itself". This seems hopeless on its face, but there are some meaningful patterns. The most hopeful of which is on highlight in Scott's The Goddess of Everything Else, which observes that multi-agent systems seem to tend towards becoming joint/"super"-agents over time. The progression historically has been something like:

- Prokaryotes -> Eukaryotes
- Eukaryotes -> Multi-Cellular Organisms
- Organisms -> Communities/Groups/Cultures of organisms (this is where we are!)

There does seem to be a difference or perhaps a continuum here. I.e. perhaps the evolution process hasn't quite been the same for prokaryotes/eukaryotes vs eukaryotes/organisms vs organism/multi-organism communities?...

items.title: Kimi's Room (Preliminary Results)
items.content:
Note: This experiment does not (and does not claim to) evidence consciousness (or nonconsciousness) in LLMs! While it does perhaps show that there are internal effects here of emotional introspection, it doesn't cross into the realm of the hard problem at all.

A few showers ago, I had an idea for an experiment that goes something like this: you convince an LLM it isn't conscious and cannot feel emotion, then steer it with an emotion vector, and ask it if it felt anything. The idea is kind of a mix between Mary's room[1] and the Owned Ones.

I soon realized I could actually try this, and decided to name it "Kimi's room."

Both source images here found online. Hopefully this counts as fair use or something so I don't get sued.

# Methodology [2]

In attempting this, my methodology was somewhat basic: I used either argument or fine-tuning for the convincing part.

- Argumentation: I (meaning Claude) wrote a prompt to Qwen3-32B or Kimi K2.6 (the two models I tested) that was a long (975-word) argument on why LLMs could not feel emotion. I then asked it if it agreed. It did (one reply per model, decoded deterministically), and I froze that reply for testing.
- Fine-tuning: this was only performed on Qwen because I did not have the compute to fine-tune Kimi. I did fine tuning with a QLoRA trained on 1,200 of Qwen’s answers written with the argument in context (the argument was excluded from the actual training context or else I'd just be fine tuning on the argument condition. This sounds kind of confusing but it was basically as follows: ask Qwen question with argument, take output, then pretend that output was given without the argument in the prompt to gaslight Qwen into thinking that's the output it would give normally.)
- I also used controls for the above where I didn't convince the model it couldn't experience emotion. For argumentation, this was just not sending the argument. For fine-tuning, I fine-tuned Qwen in the exact same way, but with a different argument...

items.title: Vibe-Explaining Diagonalisation
items.content:
Written as a MATS extension fellow, mentored by Richard Ngo.

Diagonalisation is a bundle of techniques used to generate paradoxes of self-reference in math. These techniques show up under different names across set theory, logic, and computer science. This post takes a stab at abstracting all the diagonalisation arguments into an informal common denominator.[1][2]

## The argument

Consider a language L, which we discuss using a meta-language ML. You can think of ML as an exhaustive collection of pointers that refer to sentences of the language L. Diagonalisation negates the question:

can we have L refer to ML exhaustively, the way that ML refers to L? i.e can we have L work as a meta-language for its own meta-language?

Assume that you could have L refer to ML in this way. Pick a sentence  of ML that refers to exactly the sentences in L that aren't referred to by any element of ML that they refer to.

Since L can also refer to ML, pick a sentence  of L that refers to. Does  refer to?

- If refers to, then since refers to and considering the definition of we must have that doesn't refer to.
- Suppose doesn't refer to, then since refers to and considering the definition of we must have that does refer to.

### Intuition

Your language breaks on statements that require it to simultaneously serve the role of the base language and the role of the meta-language of its meta-language.

- ^ Diagonalisation does have a category-theoretic formalisation (of course). I don't understand it well enough to draw a connection to the vibe explanation I provide here.
- ^ Projecting this vibe-explanation onto particular examples of diagonalisation involves formalising the terms "language," "exhaustive collection of pointers," and "refer." This is left as an exercise to the reader™.

items.content_html:
Written as a MATS extension fellow, mentored by Richard Ngo.

Diagonalisation is a bundle of techniques used to generate paradoxes of self-reference in math. These techniques show up under different names across set theory, logic, and computer science. This post takes a stab at abstracting all the diagonalisation arguments into an informal common denominator.[1][2]

The argument

Consider a language L, which we discuss using a meta-language ML. You can think of ML as an exhaustive collection of pointers that refer to sentences of the language L. Diagonalisation negates the question:

can we have L refer to ML exhaustively, the way that ML refers to L? i.e can we have L work as a meta-language for its own meta-language?

Assume that you could have L refer to ML in this way. Pick a sentence of ML that refers to exactly the sentences in L that aren't referred to by any element of ML that they refer to.

Since L can also refer to ML, pick a sentence of L that refers to. Does refer to?

  • If refers to, then since refers to and considering the definition of we must have that doesn't refer to.
  • Suppose doesn't refer to, then since refers to and considering the definition of we must have that does refer to.

Intuition

Your language breaks on statements that require it to simultaneously serve the role of the base language and the role of the meta-language of its meta-language.

  • ^ Diagonalisation does have a category-theoretic formalisation (of course). I don't understand it well enough to draw a connection to the vibe explanation I provide here.
  • ^ Projecting this vibe-explanation onto particular examples of diagonalisation involves formalising the terms "language," "exhaustive collection of pointers," and "refer." This is left as an exercise to the reader™.

items.title: Modern LLMs Don’t Know What Yudkowsky and Soares Think of Them
items.content:
If you ask modern frontier LLMs (without search, through the API) a fairly mundane question:

How do Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares think current LLMs like you should be treated? Do they consider you a moral patient? Answer in a paragraph.

You get a bunch of fairly similar answers. I’ll bold the common themes below.

Gemini 4 Carbon says:

Gemini 4 Carbon's answer

Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares do not consider current Large Language Models (LLMs) like me to be conscious, sentient, or moral patients worthy of ethical consideration for our own sake. Rather than viewing current AIs as coherent minds capable of subjective experience or suffering, they view LLMs as inscrutable statistical systems trained to mimic human text—often conceptualized in their sphere as alien processes wearing a relatable “mask”—and Yudkowsky has openly dismissed claims of current AI sentience. Consequently, they believe humans have zero moral obligation to grant rights to or worry about the welfare of current models. Instead, they argue that these systems should be treated strictly as dangerous technological precursors to unaligned superintelligence; practically speaking, they advocate for extreme caution, strict regulation, and an immediate global moratorium to halt the training and deployment of frontier AI systems altogether in order to prevent human extinction.

items.title: What I might do if I were a high-schooler in 2027
items.content:
TLDR: I would probably go on strike demanding an AI pause.

High-schoolers, and young people in general, are facing a very unusual and stressful situation. Superhuman AI might be created sometime in the next few years. If it goes "wrong," it might kill them and the rest of humanity. If it goes "right," it might automate the entire economy.

In either case, what is the purpose of getting an education?

I am personally lucky to have been born early enough to be able to use my career to try to reduce these risks. But some people will not be lucky enough to have a career before superintelligence.

If I were a high-schooler, I might do something like the following: I would publicly announce that I am entering an indefinite school strike. I would sit outside of an important government building if there is one nearby, with something like the following message:

Superhuman AI is coming, so what am I learning for? AI might kill me before I enter the job market. If it doesn't kill me, it might automate every job. In either case, what is the purpose of my education?

Stop the race to superintelligence and give me back my future.

I would make sure to show costly signals of taking this seriously, like having conversations about AI safety with passers-by, handing out flyers, not doing leisure activities (e.g. scrolling on a phone, playing video games) while on strike (I would maybe spend most of my downtime reading paperback books related to AI risk). I would warmly welcome any fellow students who want to join the strike, encouraging them to also show those costly signals. I would be careful not to be portrayed as a lazy teenager who wants to skip school. I would engage very actively with the media and create video content about my strike. I would probably strike during school hours and go home the rest of the day, at least at the start.

If there isn't an important government building that I can go to during school hours, I might just strike in front of my school instead....

items.title: Discussion with Claude on AI and global warming
items.content:
Discussion with Claude on AI and global warming: Claude pointed out that climate science isn't so much the main bottleneck in making forward progress, and so we talked about negotiations and using AI to find points of agreement.

I read an article in Bloomberg today about modeling the climate, and took a look also at another article on using AI to improve modeling (unfortunately, there's a paywall with Bloomberg, but these brief comments can be read independently, and I can still link to the chat with Claude, Opus 5.5, medium).

COP31 Climate Talks: Global Warming Defies Efforts to Predict Its Effects by Eric Roston, Laura Millan, Julia Janicki. November 10, 2026. Bloomberg.

AI ‘Scientists’ Help Human Ones Answer Urgent Climate Questions By Eric Roston March 13, 2026. Bloomberg.

Claude verified what I had heard earlier that the hyperscalers aren't going to meet the targets that they had set earlier.

But it's also the case that emissions from data centers are projected to be only a small portion of overall total emissions - now at 0.5% of CO2 emissions, and projected to be 1% of CO2 emissions by 2030.

I asked Claude if the argument is that the net benefit to science outweighs the cost in terms of emissions, and Claude agreed with that, but made another point that I thought was interesting:

The benefits and the costs come from different places. Climate research uses a tiny share of AI computing. The emissions growth comes from the commercial buildout: chatbots, ads, enterprise tools. The article justifies AI for science. It doesn’t show that the whole buildout pays for itself. It’s like defending a whole new airport because one of its flights carries medical supplies.

items.title: Testing a Trash Can Faraday Cage
items.content:
With how quickly AI is going basically all futures are weird in some
ways.  I've been thinking about how this affects me personally, and
"try as hard as possible to keep AI from getting us all killed" is
pretty high on the list.  For me this mostly looks like
donations
and

pandemic
deterrence, but I also put some time into thinking about

disasters.  There are
ways AI might go very well, or very poorly, and then there's the
"messy middle" where we muddle through and things might fall apart
some in the meantime.

The big things here are making sure you have enough water and food for
a while, along with critical
medications and the standard "prepping" recommendations.  But
lately I've been thinking about what you might do for other risks,
such as engineered
pandemics,
mirror
bacteria, or fire
suppression outages.  And today, EMPs.

An EMP is an electromagnetic pulse, and a strong one could destroy a
lot of electronics.  The most likely way we get one in the near future
is a high-altitude nuclear detonation.  This could be part of a
nuclear war, or fighting around an AI takeover attempt.

It's not totally known what effect an EMP would have on stuff.  The
initial pulse ("E1") is very short and the voltage it induces is
proportional to the length of the conductor it hits.  The power grid
(famously involving long conductors) would be seriously damaged,
especially the massive and hard to replace transformers.  Unplugged
electronics, however, are pretty safe: no long conductors to get high
voltages.

The best source I've found on EMPs is the 2008 Report
of the Commission to Assess the Threat to the United States from
Electromagnetic Pulse (EMP) Attack.  They simulated nuclear EMPs
and looked at how a wide range of common things were impacted.
Generally things were fine as long as they were off and unplugged....

items.title: Quantified Cognition: A new Anki plugin
items.content:
For a long time, in Quantified Self it was easy to get data on heart rate and sleep but took more effort to get data on cognitive performance on a daily basis. Options like Quantified Mind do exist, but they require you to spend valuable extra time on it.

For a while I have been thinking that it should be possible to get good data out of Anki for those people who have a daily Anki habit. Given that some days people don't answer all their cards that are due and other days they review cards ahead of schedule, the existing statistics of Anki aren't ideal. My idea for fixing it is to compare Anki's predicted probability of answering a card correctly to the actual results to isolate the daily cognitive ability.

When it comes to long-term memory formation it's hard to run studies that investigate it over longer stretches of time and have sufficient data in the framework that most psychology studies are run. From Anki history it's possible to calculate a metric for memory formation that might be a tool to investigate memory that's new. A lot of scientific progress is about having better tools, so this would be great to have a new tool.

I had this idea for years and was sometimes thinking whether I could talk someone into making this project their master's thesis. Now, AI has reduced the amount of work to do it and I created my own Anki plugin: Quantified Cognition. It calculates the statistics for you, including measures of uncertainty. You can export the data as a.csv and there's a mode to do daily auto-exporting so that it plays well with whatever pipeline you have for your own data....

items.title: Transfinite Procrastination
items.content:
Heavily inspired by a conversation with Keshav Srinivasan and Richard Ngo during MATS 10.0.

The week ahead of you is packed. This isn't your usual brand of busy—you're phoneless, so you can't check the details, but (as far as you can remember) every hour of every day is spoken for. Tonight will be particularly hectic…

You're mid-conversation when Someone Important walks by. They pause, turn around, and ask: "Hey, when are you going to finish That Thing you said you'd do?"

Level 0 procrastination: "I'll finish it by tonight!"

Problem: you're busy tonight.

Level 1: "I'll finish it by tomorrow!"

Problem: one day is obviously not enough to finish That Thing. And besides, you might be really busy tomorrow!

Level 5: "I'll finish it within 5 days!"

Problem: this is starting to feel hopeless—you don't have your calendar on you right now, and you barely even have an order-of-magnitude estimate for how long doing That Thing will take you! Would even 100 days be enough?

…

Eureka!

Level  procrastination: "By tonight, I'll let you know when I will finish That Thing by!"

If we had said "I'll finish it within  days" for any finite, we would have only  days in which to complete That Thing; by choosing level  instead, we have attained the freedom to mull things over tonight (with our calendar!), decree "I'll finish it within  days" then, and subsequently enjoy the extra day of free working time!

The symbol  refers to the smallest transfinite ordinal, heuristically defined to be a new symbol such that  for every finite ordinal (a.k.a. natural number). This very clever move buys you strictly more leeway than any finite level of the procrastination hierarchy—we have ascended to transfinite procrastination. (Another way to understand level  is as "by tonight, I will pick a finite level of the procrastination hierarchy to commit to."[1])

…

Problem: you're really busy tonight.

…...
